name: Iris Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Iris. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior buyer at Marlowe Drinks, which distributes wines, spirits and soft drinks to restaurants and bars. I start at 8 with a coffee and the overnight sales report, then taste samples or talk to vineyards and brewers about the next quarter. I use an AI assistant for drafting offers and comparing price lists, which saves me a couple of hours a day. I love a good tasting and a good deal, but the end-of-year push before the holidays is brutal.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what's your life like outside the office?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and live with my partner Tobias, who's a carpenter, in a flat above a florist on Church Street. I sing in the church choir on Thursday nights and Sundays. We've got less than a month's expenses saved, my pay at Marlowe is lower than my job title suggests, and there's really only one other drinks distributor within reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that matches what I see: useful for drafts and comparisons, not a miracle. At work I'd tell Mr Ferrand (the owner of Marlowe) that the tools I use are enough, no more spending needed. At choir I'd say nothing, because nobody asks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I'd be fine with it. I already save two hours a day and use them for calls with producers, which is where the good deals come from. My worry is the money, because Marlowe's margins are slim and hospitality is up and down. If restaurants have a bad winter, my bonus is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the assistant and build a small library of offer templates for the whole team. I'd put 150 a month into savings and Tobias would do the same, so we reach one month in the bank. I'd also ask Mr Ferrand for a title and pay review, because my title says senior but my pay says otherwise. And I'd keep visiting vineyards twice a year, since the producers remember a buyer who shows up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels fine, even a bit boring. The one thing I feel is the money, every time a bill arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What would 'mostly hype' mean for that habit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said producers remember the buyer who shows up. Can you give me an example?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the hours it saves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring I drove four hours to a small family vineyard that was about to be dropped by another distributor. Madame Roche (the vineyard owner) gave me a better price on 600 cases than any email would have. We still talk every month.

say: I'd say AI is **useful but no miracle**, and our tools are enough.
I'd tell Mr Ferrand (the owner of Marlowe) we don't need to **spend more**.
think: I'm fine with it, since I already save **two hours a day** on offers.
A **bad winter** for restaurants could wipe out my bonus.
do: Build a library of **offer templates** for the whole team.
Put **150 a month** into savings, matched by Tobias.
Ask Mr Ferrand for a **pay review**, because my title says senior and my pay doesn't.
feel: **Fine** and a bit boring, apart from the stab when bills arrive.
S0.quote: Madame Roche (the vineyard owner) gave me a better price on 600 cases than any email would have.
fieldNote: Already an **everyday AI user**, so a mild scenario costs her nothing.
Worries come from low pay and a **shaky hospitality market**.
Uses relationships with producers as her real edge.

steps.text: Build a library of offer templates for the team
Put 150 a month into savings with Tobias
Ask Mr Ferrand for a pay and title review

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be uncomfortable but fair, as long as companies let people learn on the job. At work I'd offer to run a lunch-and-learn on the tools for the other buyers. At church I'd say we should help families who feel the pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my own desk changes most. Comparing price lists, drafting offers, booking orders and answering customers is nearly all my day, and the software gets better every month. Marlowe now has three buyers, and with these tools one person could do much more, so I'd guess the team shrinks to two within three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the one who understands the system by building a better version for Marlowe and showing Mr Ferrand the time saved. I'd also take a short course in negotiation and category strategy, because the human part of buying will matter more. Tobias's work is hands-on, and his firm has plenty of orders, so we'd lean on his income if mine wobbled. I'd start a small side project too, a monthly wine box for local customers, to see if I can sell directly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a rising tide. I'm curious, but I'd be lying if I said I wasn't scared. The low pay makes a layoff more painful because I'm not saving much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of those tasks do you think goes first at Marlowe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which would you rather do: be one of the two buyers left, or run your own wine box?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Tobias's work fit in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two buyers, if I'm honest, because the pay would be steadier. But I'd run the box on the side, because I wouldn't want my whole life tied to one boss. Tobias (my partner) keeps telling me a person with two incomes is never stuck.

say: I'd say it's **uncomfortable but fair** if people can learn on the job.
I'd offer a **lunch-and-learn** on the tools for the other buyers.
think: Comparing prices, drafting offers and booking orders are nearly all my day, so my desk is **first in line**.
Marlowe's three buyers could shrink to **two** within three years.
do: Build a **better version** of the system for Marlowe and show the time saved.
Take a short course in **negotiation and category strategy**.
Start a monthly **wine box** for local customers as a side income.
feel: Like a **rising tide**: curious, but scared too, with low pay and little saved.
S1.quote: Tobias (my partner) keeps telling me a person with two incomes is never stuck.
fieldNote: Moves first: **builds, teaches and sells** instead of waiting.
Expects the buying team to shrink from three to two.
Her partner's hands-on job and her side income give her a second leg.

steps.text: Build a better buying assistant for Marlowe and show Mr Ferrand
Take a negotiation and category strategy course
Start a monthly wine box for local customers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is moving too fast, and we should slow down and look after people. At work I'd tell Mr Ferrand, plainly, that Marlowe needs a plan for buyers within six months. At church I'd ask us to check on each other, because many families here depend on office jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my desk goes. Buying is the sort of thinking an AI does well, and I use it every day, so I know how good it is. Because I'm already on lower pay, Marlowe has little reason to keep me when a system does the job, and there's no other big distributor nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First call is Mr Ferrand, to offer to run the system that replaces the team, because I know it better than anyone. Second is my aunt, who owns a small restaurant, to ask about work in her kitchen and front of house, because hands-on jobs last until about 2031. We'd cut everything but rent and groceries, and Tobias would take extra jobs. I'd also begin selling the wine box seriously, to restaurants I already know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels frightening. I'd also feel strangely prepared, because I've seen how fast the tools improve. But I'd be afraid for Tobias and me, because we have almost nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first call you make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you say to Tobias that night?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Tobias talk about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got hands that can build and a head that knows the tools, so we're not helpless. But I'm scared, because pretending I'm not would be a lie. He'd probably say, let's make dinner and plan after.

say: I'd say this is moving **too fast** and we should look after people.
I'd tell Mr Ferrand (the owner) plainly that Marlowe needs a **plan for buyers** within six months.
think: Buying is thinking work I know AI does well, so my **desk goes**.
With no other big distributor nearby, there is **little reason** to keep me.
do: Offer to **run the system** that replaces the buying team.
Ask my aunt about work in her **restaurant**, since hands-on jobs last to about 2031.
Cut to **rent and groceries** and sell the wine box to restaurants.
feel: **Frightened**, yet oddly prepared, and afraid for Tobias and me.
S2.quote: We've got hands that can build and a head that knows the tools, so we're not helpless. But I'm scared, because pretending I'm not would be a lie.
fieldNote: Knows how good the tools are, so **expects to lose** the desk.
Lines up three fallbacks: running the system, her aunt's restaurant, the wine box.
Honest about fear; uses partner and family as support.

steps.text: Offer to run the system that replaces the buying team
Ask my aunt for work at her restaurant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a warning we should use, and companies should be honest with staff about it. At work I'd tell Mr Ferrand to start moving buyers into producer relations and sales. At church I'd say prepare, don't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose the pure buying job, but five years is enough to be somewhere else. I'd rather jump than be pushed. My biggest risk isn't skill but money, because I can't take a pay cut with so little saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd save 200 a month and build the wine box to ten customers. By year two I'd apply to producers and brewers who want a sales or export person, since the human side of selling lasts longer. Tobias and I would postpone the wedding by a year, and I'd keep using the AI tools every day so I'm quicker than anyone else. And if the box makes enough, I'd think about a small shop-and-tasting room with a friend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long hallway with a door at the end. I'd be worried, but I'd also be busy, and busy feels better than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd postpone the wedding. How would Tobias feel about that?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd start this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be disappointed, but he'd get it. We both grew up with parents who saved first and celebrated second. He'd rather marry with a cushion than borrow for a party.

say: I'd say it's a **warning** we should use, and companies should be honest about it.
I'd tell Mr Ferrand (the owner) to move buyers into **producer relations** and sales.
think: I'd lose the pure buying job, but five years is enough to be **somewhere else**.
My biggest risk is **money**, because I can't take a pay cut.
do: Save **200 a month** and grow the wine box to ten customers.
Apply to **producers and brewers** who want a sales person by year two.
feel: Like a **long hallway** with a door at the end, busy rather than waiting.
S3.quote: I'd rather jump than be pushed. My biggest risk isn't skill but money, because I can't take a pay cut with so little saved.
fieldNote: Jumps early: sees **sales and producer roles** as the next stage.
Her anxiety is money, not skill.

steps.text: Save 200 a month toward a three-month cushion
Grow the wine box to ten regular customers
Apply for sales roles with producers and brewers by year two
Postpone the wedding by a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do this well, with training and fair rules. At work I'd tell Mr Ferrand to hire a junior and teach them both the tools and the people side. At church I'd say keep the community strong, because that's what lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think ten years is plenty of time for someone like me. I'm good with the tools, I like people, and I'd have savings. I'd feel fairly safe, though I'm still on a lower pay and don't want to wait too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off my studies in four years and build six months of savings in two. I'd move from pure buying to a role that mixes buying with supplier relations, maybe at a producer. I'd keep growing the wine box until it pays a few hundred a month. And Tobias and I would marry in about three years and think about children after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good, even a bit exciting. The money still pinches today, but a long runway makes it feel solvable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to achieve by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you don't want to wait too long. What does that mean?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is ten years too long to feel urgent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I don't trust a long runway not to turn into a long nap. I'd set a date, like next autumn, to apply for the first producer job. I'd tell Tobias and my aunt so they'd ask me about it.

say: I'd say ten years is time to do it **well**, with training and fair rules.
I'd tell Mr Ferrand (the owner) to hire a **junior** and teach both tools and people skills.
think: Ten years is **plenty** for someone good with the tools and with people.
I'm on lower pay, so I don't want to **wait too long**.
do: Pay off my **studies** in four years and build six months of savings in two.
Move into a role mixing buying and **supplier relations**, maybe at a producer.
Marry Tobias in about **three years**, then think about children.
feel: **Good**, even a bit exciting, with money that still pinches.
S4.quote: I don't trust a long runway not to turn into a long nap. I'd set a date, like next autumn, to apply for the first producer job.
fieldNote: Uses a **deadline** and her aunt's questions to avoid drifting.
Plans marriage and children after the cushion exists.
Uneasy, not calm, since her pay remains low.

steps.text: Pay off the student loan within four years
Apply for a first producer relations job by next autumn
Marry Tobias in about three years and plan children after

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I can use the tools, but I couldn't turn that into a new income in time, with nothing saved. What would help is a clear notice before companies change, a tax break or grant for people retraining on their own, and honest bosses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say don't forget the people who are good with the new tools. We look okay from the outside, but we're often the ones who will be asked to build the thing that replaces our own team. That's an odd position to be in at 27.

headlineQuote: We're often the ones who will be asked to build the thing that replaces our own team. That's an odd position to be in at 27.
portrait: Iris is a 27-year-old senior buyer at a **drinks distributor**, living with her partner Tobias, a carpenter.
She is on lower pay, has **under a month** saved, and sees only one other distributor nearby.
She is traditional, sings in her church choir, and uses **AI every day**.
In the fast worlds she expects to lose her desk and lines up a **restaurant job** and a wine box.
With time she moves from buying into **supplier relations** and sales.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries her most, because she couldn't build a new income in time.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **notice** from companies, grants for self-funded retraining, and honest bosses.
